title: SEO for a Gin Brand | Craft Beer School
desc: SEO for a gin brand: how people search for gin, pages for botanicals and cocktails, a where-to-buy page and alcohol advertising rules to respect.
teaser: Gin drinkers search for botanicals, cocktails and where to buy. A small brand can serve all three without a large budget.
standfirst: A gin brand competes with big names for broad searches, so the practical aim is narrower: be the clear answer to specific questions about your gin.
sections:
Some search by name when they have heard of a brand. Some search for a style or a flavour, such as a citrus-led gin. Many search for a drink, such as a gin and tonic recipe. A few search for where to buy.

A new brand will not win the broad terms quickly. Nobody can promise that it will. Aim at the specific ones you can answer better than anyone: your own name, your botanicals and your serves.

• A page for each gin with botanicals, strength, tasting notes and serve suggestions.
  • A story page about the distillery and how the gin is made.
  • A stockists page that lists where to buy, with names and areas.
  • A cocktails page with a few recipes you stand behind.
  • A contact and trade enquiry page.

The stockists page matters a lot. Many searches end in a question of where to buy. An honest list answers it.

Write about the botanicals you use. Juniper is the defining one in gin. People also search for coriander, citrus peel and local botanicals. Explain what each adds to the taste in plain words. If you use a local ingredient, say where it comes from.

Recipes bring visitors, but write them properly: quantities in millilitres, ice, garnish and method. Test them. Give a non-alcoholic serve too, for guests who do not drink. Choose which recipes to write by checking what people really type, using the method in our keyword research guide.
Your brand name is a search problem

If your gin has a common word as its name, searchers may see unrelated results. Add context: always write the full name with the word gin and your location in titles and descriptions. Check what appears when you search for your own name. Make your site and profiles occupy that space.

Set up a Google Business Profile if you have a distillery door or tasting room. If not, a profile may not be allowed, so check Google's rules.

Rules about promoting and selling spirits are strict and differ by country and, in India, by state. Some places restrict alcohol advertising online. Some restrict e-commerce altogether. Do not target under-age audiences, show consumption in unsafe settings or imply health benefits. Add a responsible drinking message. If unsure, ask the regulator or a lawyer.

Check Search Console each month for the searches that show your site. Note which pages get impressions but few clicks, since their titles may need rewriting. Look at your stockists page: if people reach it and leave, add detail or fix broken links.

Link to your site from places that are real: stockists, bars that serve your gin, local press and your social profiles. Do not buy links in bulk, since that breaks search engine rules and can harm your site.

Keep an eye on the pace. A new brand's site may take months to show steady results. A few good pages tied to real stockists are better than a large site full of filler. Keep a log of what you publish so you can tie changes in visits to your actions.

A practical routine helps. Once a month, pick one page, read it as a stranger, fix the unclear parts and check that every claim is true. Also check that the age statement and responsible drinking line appear where local rules need them. Small steady edits beat a big rewrite you never finish. They keep your pages accurate as ranges, stockists and prices change.

Ask your stockists and bars to link to your site from their pages where they are happy to. A link from a real venue that serves your gin is a sign of a real brand. It also sends curious visitors to you.

Week one: audit your pages and fix titles, descriptions and basic facts. Week two: write the stockists page. Week three: publish two cocktail or botanical pages. Week four: set up tracking and read Search Console. Plan the next steps from what you see. Also read SEO for breweries, whose basics apply to any drinks site.
faqs: Can a new gin brand rank for gin?
Broad searches are competitive and no one can promise a position. Focus on specific searches where you have the best answer.
Yes, if you are happy to share them. Searchers look for them and it builds trust.
Not always. If selling online is not allowed or practical, a clear where-to-buy page still serves the visitor.
